Report the methods and the decisions of an analysis

Source: R/report.R
report_interactions.Rd

Writes, from the output of estimate_interactions(), the methods of the statistical analysis as paragraphs of text and a table with every decision behind it: the design, the model of each response, the null models and why they were chosen, the inference and, when given, the classification of the interactions and the agreement among null models. The text cites the methods used and lists their references. Every value comes from the settings of the objects, so the description matches the analysis that was run.

Usage

report_interactions(x, classes = NULL, agreement = NULL, justification = NULL)

Arguments

x

The output of estimate_interactions().

classes

Optional: the output of classify_interactions() for x, to describe the classification of the interactions.

agreement

Optional: the output of compare_null_models() for x, to describe the agreement among the null models.

justification

Optional text, one or more sentences, that justifies the choice of null models; it is added to the methods as given. When the null models came from suggest_null_models(), the criteria behind them are described without it.

Value

An object of class must_report, a list with methods (the paragraphs, a character vector), decisions (a data frame with columns step, decision, argument, value, default and source) and references (the works cited, formatted, a character vector). format() gives the whole report as lines of plain text or, with format = "markdown", of markdown for an R Markdown or Quarto document (in a chunk with results = "asis"); print() shows the plain text.

Details

The methods have up to five paragraphs: the design (stressors, units, times and the interactions the design identifies); the software and the model of each response (for a model fitted with fit_responses(), the candidates for its error distribution, how one was chosen and the random effects; for a model fitted outside must, its class and family); the null models and why they were chosen (the criteria of suggest_null_models(), the justification given or, for the default, why it is the default); how the interactions were estimated and tested; and, when classes or agreement are given, how the interactions were classified and compared. They are written in English, in the past tense, for the methods section of a manuscript, and are meant to be edited: the description of the experiment itself (organisms, exposure, measurements) is left to the authors.

The table of decisions has one row per decision, with the function (step) and argument that control it, the value used, the default and its source: "default", "set" (given by the user), "chosen" (by must: the distribution selected by fit_responses(), a seed drawn at random), "estimated" (criteria of suggest_null_models() evaluated from the effects estimated), "suggest_null_models()" (the null models suggested) or "recorded" (versions of the software). The versions are those recorded when the models were fitted and the interactions estimated; objects created by earlier versions of must lack them and the summary of the models, and the report then says less.

See also

estimate_interactions(), suggest_null_models(), classify_interactions(), compare_null_models().

Examples

jars <- expand.grid(
  salinity = c("ambient", "high"),
  warming = c("no", "yes"),
  replicate = 1:5,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
jars$jar <- seq_len(nrow(jars))
mu <- 40 * ifelse(jars$salinity == "high", 0.5, 1) *
  ifelse(jars$warming == "yes", 0.5, 1)
jars$algae <- stats::qpois(c(0.2, 0.35, 0.5, 0.65, 0.8)[jars$replicate], mu)
design <- describe_design(jars, c("salinity", "warming"),
  control = c(salinity = "ambient", warming = "no"), unit = "jar")
fits <- fit_responses(jars, "algae", design, residual_checks = FALSE,
  seed = 1, quiet = TRUE)
est <- estimate_interactions(fits, null_models = c("AD", "MU"), n_sim = 2000,
  seed = 1)
report <- report_interactions(est, classes = classify_interactions(est))
report
#> <must_report>
#> Methods
#> 
#> The experiment combined 2 stressors, salinity (ambient and high, with ambient
#> as control) and warming (no and yes, with no as control), in a full factorial
#> design (4 treatment combinations), with 5 experimental units (jar) per
#> combination. The design identified one contrast set, a pairwise interaction.
#> 
#> The analysis was run with the R package must 0.2.0 (Amador Crespo 2026) in R
#> 4.6.2 (R Core Team 2026). The response (algae) was modelled with a generalized
#> linear model with one mean per treatment combination (a cell-means model),
#> fitted by maximum likelihood with glmmTMB 1.1.15.2 (Brooks et al. 2017). The
#> error distribution was chosen among candidates suited to the values of the
#> response (Poisson (log link) and negative binomial (NB2, log link)): the
#> candidate that converged with a positive-definite Hessian and had the lowest
#> AIC was selected, except that the Poisson was used only if the negative
#> binomial did not converge. The model selected was negative binomial (NB2, log
#> link). For the inference, the selected model was refitted by restricted maximum
#> likelihood (REML).
#> 
#> Each interaction was tested against simple addition (AD) and the multiplicative
#> model (MU). Following Madge Pimentel et al. (2025), each interaction was
#> computed from the means predicted by the model (post-estimation inference), as
#> the deviation of the combination of stressors from the expectation of the null
#> model, as a difference on the scale of the response (AD) and as a difference on
#> the log scale (MU). Uncertainty was obtained from 2,000 draws of the fixed
#> effects from their estimated distribution (Krinsky & Robb 1986), which gave
#> percentile intervals and two-sided p-values. To correct for small samples, the
#> covariance came from the REML refit and the distributions were t, with the
#> degrees of freedom given by the replication of the experimental units (16).
#> Intervals were computed at the 95% level, and p-values were adjusted for the
#> false discovery rate (Benjamini & Hochberg 1995) within each response, null
#> model and estimate, across contrast sets. Random numbers were generated with
#> seed 1.
#> 
#> Interactions were classified with the directional scheme of Piggott et al.
#> (2015): each single, combined and interaction effect was coded as positive,
#> negative or not significant from its adjusted p-value (alpha = 0.05), and each
#> net interaction was classed as additive (no deviation detected), as a positive
#> or negative synergism or as a positive or negative antagonism (their Table 1).
#> 
#> Decisions
#> 
#> describe_design()
#>   Stressors and their control levels: salinity (control ambient), warming
#>     (control no) [stressors, control, set]
#>   Experimental unit: jar [unit, set]
#>   Sampling time: none [time, default]
#>   Groups of units (blocks, rooms, whole plots): none [groups, default]
#>   Factors within which interactions are estimated: none [by, default]
#>   Level of the stressors outside each set: control [background, default]
#>   Highest number of stressors in a set: 2 (all stressors) [max_order, default]
#> 
#> fit_responses()
#>   Candidate distributions (algae): Poisson (log link) and negative binomial
#>     (NB2, log link) (count, detected) [families, default]
#>   Observations that share a dispersion parameter: common [dispersion, default]
#>   Random effects: automatic: none [random, default]
#>   Limits of the optimiser: scaled iteration limits [control, default]
#>   Residual checks with DHARMa: FALSE [residual_checks, set]
#>   Distribution selected (algae): negative binomial (NB2, log link) [chosen]
#>

#> The experiment combined 2 stressors, salinity (ambient and high, with ambient as control) and warming (no and yes, with no as control), in a full factorial design (4 treatment combinations), with 5 experimental units (jar) per combination. The design identified one contrast set, a pairwise interaction.
#> 
#> The analysis was run with the R package must 0.2.0 (Amador Crespo 2026) in R 4.6.2 (R Core Team 2026). The response (algae) was modelled with a generalized linear model with one mean per treatment combination (a cell-means model), fitted by maximum likelihood with glmmTMB 1.1.15.2 (Brooks et al. 2017). The error distribution was chosen among candidates suited to the values of the response (Poisson (log link) and negative binomial (NB2, log link)): the candidate that converged with a positive-definite Hessian and had the lowest AIC was selected, except that the Poisson was used only if the negative binomial did not converge. The model selected was negative binomial (NB2, log link). For the inference, the selected model was refitted by restricted maximum likelihood (REML).
#> 
#> Each interaction was tested against simple addition (AD) and the multiplicative model (MU). Following Madge Pimentel et al. (2025), each interaction was computed from the means predicted by the model (post-estimation inference), as the deviation of the combination of stressors from the expectation of the null model, as a difference on the scale of the response (AD) and as a difference on the log scale (MU). Uncertainty was obtained from 2,000 draws of the fixed effects from their estimated distribution (Krinsky & Robb 1986), which gave percentile intervals and two-sided p-values. To correct for small samples, the covariance came from the REML refit and the distributions were t, with the degrees of freedom given by the replication of the experimental units (16). Intervals were computed at the 95% level, and p-values were adjusted for the false discovery rate (Benjamini & Hochberg 1995) within each response, null model and estimate, across contrast sets. Random numbers were generated with seed 1.
#> 
#> Interactions were classified with the directional scheme of Piggott et al. (2015): each single, combined and interaction effect was coded as positive, negative or not significant from its adjusted p-value (alpha = 0.05), and each net interaction was classed as additive (no deviation detected), as a positive or negative synergism or as a positive or negative antagonism (their Table 1).
